# Abstract {.unnumbered} 

Missing data complicate inference throughout the health and social sciences, and the difficulty is amplified in cluster-randomized trials (CRTs), where intact groups rather than individuals are assigned to treatment. Shared environments induce dependence among observations within clusters, so standard analyses that ignore clustering understate uncertainty and distort effective sample size. Multiple imputation (MI) addresses incomplete data by generating several completed datasets, fitting the substantive model to each, and combining the resulting estimates through Rubin's rules; in clustered settings, the imputation model itself must preserve that dependence structure. This thesis focuses on a quantity that sits at the center of CRT design and analysis: the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), which measures the share of total outcome variance attributable to between-cluster differences. Although Rubin's rules are routinely applied to scalar parameters after MI, they are most reliable when the complete-data estimator is approximately normal on the scale being pooled. ICC estimates are bounded on $[0,1]$, often skewed, and can accumulate at the boundary when variance components are constrained to be nonnegative, so raw-scale pooling may yield poorly calibrated standard errors and intervals that stray outside the parameter space. We therefore investigate whether transforming the ICC before pooling---and back-transforming afterward---improves the operating characteristics of MI-based inference relative to leaving the ICC on its original scale. Candidate transformations include Fisher's $z$, the logit, the arcsine square-root, and related log-based and Freeman--Tukey variants, none of which is a priori guaranteed to dominate for this parameter. Using a simulation study built around a continuous-outcome random-intercept mixed model with known true ICC, induced missingness, and MI, we will evaluate each strategy by bias, empirical variance, mean squared error, and confidence-interval coverage, and we will complement the simulation with an applied illustration from a real CRT. The broader aim is to clarify when conventional Rubin pooling of the ICC is adequate and when a carefully chosen transformation yields more faithful estimates and intervals.
